NOTE 1: The steps above apply to interworking with N26. - Step 14a: - If the AMF does not have event subscription information from the UDM, the AMF indicates it in Nudm\_UECM\_Registration. evidence.text: ... ine if mobility of the UE to 5GS or NR connected to 5GS should be permitted. If the SMF+PGW-C receives the PDU session ID from UE via PCO and know 5GC is not restricted for the PDN connection by user subscription, the SMF+PGW-C sends the mapped QoS parameters to UE. When the UE moves from EPS to 5GS, for the case when the MME has selected SMF+PGW-C even for PDN connections that cannot be relocated to the target 5GS, the SMF+PGW-C determines which PDN Connections can be relocated to the target 5GS, e.g. based on capability of the deployed 5GS, subscription and operator policies for which PDN Connection, seamless session continuity should be supported etc. The SMF+PGW-C and NG-RAN can reject the PDN Connections that cannot be transferred as part of the handover or Idle mode mobility. For the case when the MME has selected standalone P-GW for a PDN connection for which session continuity is not supported and the AMF cannot retrieve the address of the corresponding SMF during EPS to 5GS mobility, the AMF does not move the PDN connection to 5GS. NOTE 2: When applying the AMF planned removal procedure or the procedure to handle AMF failures (see clause 5.21.2) implementations are expected to update the DNS configuration to enable MMEs to discover alternative AMFs if the MME tries to retrieve a UE context from an AMF that has been taken out of service or has failed. This addresses the scenario of UEs performing 5GS to EPS Idle mode mobility and presenting a mapped GUTI pointing to an AMF that has been taken out of service or has failed. In the case of mobility from 5GS to EPS, if the MME lacks certain capability, e.g. MME not supporting 15 EPS bearers, the 5GC shall not transfer the UE EPS bearers and/or EPS PDN connections that are not supported by the EPC network. If the MME does not support 15 EPS bearers, the AMF determines which EBIs cannot be transferred to EPS, and retrieves the EPS bearer contexts from the SMF+PGW-C for the EBIs that can be transferred to EPS. NOTE 3: How the AMF determines which EBIs can be transferred to EPS is according to local configuration, e.g. according to DNN, S-NSSAI, ARP associated with an EBI. Definitions and abbreviations ### 3.1 Definitions For the purposes of the present document, the terms and definitions given in TR 21.905 [1], TS 23.502 [3], TS 23.503 [45] and the following apply. A term defined in the present document takes precedence over the definition of the same term, if any, in TR 21.905 [1]. **5G VN Group:** A set of UEs using private communication for 5G LAN-type service. **5G Access Network:** An access network comprising a NG-RAN and/or non-3GPP AN connecting to a 5G Core Network. **5G Access Stratum-based Time Distribution:** A time synchronization distribution method that is used by an NG-RAN to provide the 5GS time to the UE(s) over the radio interface using procedures specified in TS 38.331 [28]. **5G Core Network:** The core network specified in the present document. It connects to a 5G Access Network. **5G LAN-Type Service:** A service over the 5G system offering private communication using IP and/or non-IP type communications. **5G LAN-Virtual Network:** A virtual network over the 5G system capable of supporting 5G LAN-type service. **5G NSWO:** The 5G NSWO is the capability provided by 5G system and by UE to enable the connection to a WLAN access network using 5GS credentials without registration to 5GS. **5G QoS Flow or QoS Flow:** The finest granularity for QoS forwarding treatment in the 5G System. All traffic mapped to the same 5G QoS Flow receive the same forwarding treatment (e.g. scheduling policy, queue management policy, rate shaping policy, RLC configuration, etc.). Providing different QoS forwarding treatment requires separate 5G QoS Flow. **5G QoS Identifier:** A scalar that is used as a reference to a specific QoS forwarding behaviour (e.g. packet loss rate, packet delay budget) to be provided to a 5G QoS Flow. This may be implemented in the access network by the 5QI referencing node specific parameters that control the QoS forwarding treatment (e.g. scheduling weights, admission thresholds, queue management thresholds, link layer protocol configuration, etc.). **5G System:** 3GPP system consisting of 5G Access Network (AN), 5G Core Network and UE. **5G-BRG:** The 5G-BRG is a 5G-RG defined in BBF. **5G-CRG:** The 5G-CRG is a 5G-RG specified in DOCSIS MULPI [89]. **5G-RG:** A 5G-RG is a RG capable of connecting to 5GC playing the role of a UE with regard to the 5G core. Q1.answer:
In a 5G Standalone (SA) network, the Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF) serves as the central anchor for control plane signaling related to UE registration, connection management, and mobility. Based on the provided 3GPP specifications, the AMF’s specific roles in registration and mobility management are detailed below.

### 1. Registration Management
The AMF is the primary network function responsible for handling the Registration Procedure, which establishes the UE’s presence in the 5G System (5GS).

*   **Processing Registration Requests:** The AMF receives the Registration Request from the UE (via the NG-RAN) and processes it based on the registration type (e.g., Initial Registration, Periodic Registration, or Mobility Registration) [E2].
*   **Interaction with UDM:** During registration, the AMF interacts with the Unified Data Management (UDM) to retrieve subscription data and update the UE’s location information. Specifically, the AMF uses the `Nudm_UECM_Registration` service to register the UE with the UDM. If the AMF lacks event subscription information, it indicates this to the UDM, which then provides any necessary event subscriptions (potentially retrieved from the Unified Data Repository, UDR) [E2].
*   **Handling Interworking Scenarios:** In cases involving interworking with Evolved Packet Core (EPC), the AMF manages the mapping of identifiers. For an Initial Registration where the UE provides a 5G-GUTI mapped from an EPS GUTI, the AMF may need to perform an Identification Request towards the MME (in N26 interworking scenarios) to verify the EPS Attach Request [E2].
*   **Access Type Registration:** When mobility between GERAN/UTRAN and 5GS is required, the AMF serving the 3GPP access must register with the UDM even if it already holds a valid context, ensuring the UDM stores the associated 3GPP Access Type along with the serving AMF [E2].

### 2. Mobility Management
The AMF manages the mobility of UEs between different access networks and within the 5GS, ensuring session continuity and proper context transfer.

*   **Interworking with EPC (N26 and Non-N26):** The AMF plays a critical role in mobility between 5GS and EPC.
    *   **5GS to EPS Mobility:** If a UE moves from 5GS to EPS, the AMF determines which Evolved Bearers (EBIs) can be transferred to the EPC based on local configuration (e.g., DNN, S-NSSAI, ARP). It retrieves the EPS bearer contexts from the SMF+PGW-C for the transferable EBIs [E3].
    *   **EPS to 5GS Mobility:** When a UE moves from EPS to 5GS, the AMF facilitates the relocation of PDN connections. If the AMF cannot retrieve the address of the corresponding SMF for a PDN connection (e.g., if a standalone P-GW was selected and session continuity is not supported), the AMF does not move that specific PDN connection to the 5GS [E3].
    *   **Context Retrieval:** In N26 interworking, the AMF may retrieve UE context from the MME to support mobility procedures [E2].
*   **Mobility between 5GS and GERAN/UTRAN:** The AMF supports mobility between 5GS and legacy 2G/3G networks (GERAN/UTRAN). Upon registration, the AMF ensures that the UDM cancels any other previously registered serving nodes (such as an MME or SGSN) via the HSS/HLR to maintain a single active registration point for the UE [E2].
*   **AMF Failure and Planned Removal:** The AMF is involved in resilience procedures. If an AMF is taken out of service or fails, implementations are expected to update DNS configurations to enable MMEs to discover alternative AMFs. This is crucial for UEs performing 5GS to EPS idle mode mobility that present a mapped GUTI pointing to a failed or removed AMF [E3].
*   **Policy-Driven Mobility:** The AMF may receive Route Selection Policy (RFSP) updates from the Policy Control Function (PCF). If the PCF modifies the RFSP Index to prioritize EPC/E-UTRAN access over 5GS access, the AMF may receive an RFSP in Use Validity Time, influencing its mobility management decisions [E3].

### 3. Architectural Context
The AMF is a core network function within the 5G Core Network (5GC), which connects to the 5G Access Network (comprising NG-RAN and/or non-3GPP AN) [E1]. It operates alongside other network functions such as

This can be done by, for example, the AMF providing a back-off time to the UE, such as described in clause 5.19.7.2 NAS level congestion control. The AMF shall be prepared to deregister the UE if the information received from LMF indicates that the UE is registered to a PLMN that is not allowed to operate in the UE location. In a 5G network, inter-gNB handover is a mobility procedure where a User Equipment (UE) in RRC_CONNECTED state moves from a source gNB to a target gNB. The procedure involves coordination between the source gNB, the target gNB, and the Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF) to ensure seamless session continuity and context transfer.

**1. Measurement and Handover Decision (Source gNB)**
The source gNB initiates the process by configuring the UE to perform measurements on neighboring cells. The UE reports measurement results, such as Reference Signal Received Power (RSRP) or Reference Signal Received Quality (RSRQ), to the source gNB [E2]. Based on these reports and network configuration, the source gNB makes the handover decision. If the target cell is served by a different gNB, an inter-gNB handover is triggered. The source gNB may also utilize CSI-RS based mobility, where neighboring gNBs exchange and forward their own CSI-RS configurations to facilitate this decision [E2].

**2. Handover Preparation (Source gNB to Target gNB via AMF)**
Once the decision is made, the source gNB sends a **HANDOVER REQUEST** message to the target gNB. This message is routed via the AMF over the N2 interface. The HANDOVER REQUEST contains:
*   **UE Context:** Information necessary for the target gNB to prepare resources, including PDU session information, QoS flows, and security parameters.
*   **Mobility Restriction List:** If present, the target gNB uses this list to determine subsequent mobility targets, select Serving Cell Groups (SCG) in dual connectivity, or assign RAN Areas (RNA) for RRC_INACTIVE state [E4].
*   **Trace Activation:** If included, the target gNB initiates the requested trace function [E4].
*   **Forwarding Indication:** The source gNB may indicate whether it supports direct or indirect data forwarding. If indirect forwarding is applied, the target gNB may admit the forwarding of downlink data for specific QoS flows [E4].

**3. Handover Admission (Target gNB)**
The target gNB evaluates the request based on available resources and admission control. If the target gNB admits the handover, it allocates radio resources and prepares the UE context. It then sends a **HANDOVER REQUEST ACKNOWLEDGE** message back to the source gNB via the AMF. This message includes:
*   **RRC Reconfiguration Message:** A transparent container containing the RRC Reconfiguration message that the source gNB will send to the UE to command the handover.
*   **DL Forwarding UP TNL Information:** If indirect data forwarding is accepted for at least one QoS flow, the target gNB includes this information to enable the source gNB to forward downlink data to the target [E4].
*   **NPN Access Information:** If the target cell is a Closed Access Group (CAG) cell, the target gNB includes this information, which the AMF uses to verify access permissions [E4].

**4. Handover Execution (Source gNB to UE)**
Upon receiving the acknowledgment, the source gNB sends the **RRC Reconfiguration** message to the UE, instructing it to switch to the target cell. The UE synchronizes with the target gNB and sends an RRC Reconfiguration Complete message to the target gNB.

**5. Handover Completion and Context Release**
*   **Data Forwarding:** If configured, the source gNB forwards any buffered downlink data to the target gNB via the path indicated in the HANDOVER REQUEST ACKNOWLEDGE (direct or indirect) [E4].
*   **Context Release:** The target gNB notifies the AMF that the handover is complete. The AMF then sends a **UE CONTEXT RELEASE** command to the source gNB to free up resources.
*   **AMF Role in Location and Access:** Throughout the process, the AMF may verify the UE's location based on the ULI (including Cell ID) received from the gNB. If the AMF determines the UE is not allowed to operate in the new location (e.g., due to regulatory or licensing constraints), it may reject the handover or accept it and subsequently deregister the UE [E3][E5]. Additionally, the AMF manages the UE's registration area and may trigger an AMF change if the target gNB is served by a different AMF, though the core handover signaling between gNBs remains as described.

**Summary of Roles:**
*   **Source gNB:** Initiates handover based on UE measurements, sends HANDOVER REQUEST, forwards data, and releases resources.

Q3.answer:
In a 5G NR network, Radio Link Failure (RLF) is detected through a combination of physical layer out-of-sync indications and higher-layer protocol failures, and is handled via specific recovery procedures defined in 3GPP TS 38.331.

### Detection of Radio Link Failure

The detection process is hierarchical, starting with physical layer monitoring and escalating to RRC-level failure declaration based on timer expirations and protocol errors.

**1. Physical Layer Problem Detection (Out-of-Sync)**
The UE monitors the physical layer quality of the Special Cell (SpCell).
*   **Trigger:** The UE starts timer **T310** upon receiving **N310** consecutive "out-of-sync" indications from the lower layers for the SpCell [E2].
*   **Condition:** This typically occurs when timers T300, T301, T304, T311, T316, or T319 are not running [E2].
*   **Recovery from Physical Layer Issues:** If the UE receives **N311** consecutive "in-sync" indications while T310 is running, it stops T310 (and T312 if running) and maintains the RRC connection without explicit signalling [E2].

**2. Declaration of Radio Link Failure**
If the physical layer issues are not resolved, or if higher-layer failures occur, the UE declares RLF. The UE considers RLF detected for the Master Cell Group (MCG) under the following conditions [E2]:
*   **T310 Expiry:** Timer T310 expires for the SpCell.
*   **Random Access Problem:** An indication of a random access problem is received from the MCG MAC layer.
*   **RLC Retransmission Limit:** An indication from the MCG RLC layer that the maximum number of retransmissions has been reached.
*   **Uplink LBT Failure:** A consistent uplink Listen-Before-Talk (LBT) failure indication from the MCG MAC layer.

*Note: For Dual Active Protocol Stack (DAPS) bearers, specific conditions involving T304 and source SpCell/MCG indications also trigger RLF detection for the source MCG [E2].*

### Handling of Radio Link Failure

Upon detecting RLF, the UE executes specific actions to clean up the current connection and initiate recovery.

**1. Immediate Actions upon RLF Detection**
When RLF is detected (e.g., for the source MCG in DAPS scenarios or generally for the MCG), the UE performs the following [E2]:
*   **Suspend Data:** Suspend transmission and reception of all Data Radio Bearers (DRBs) and multicast MRBs in the affected MCG.
*   **Reset MAC:** Reset the Medium Access Control (MAC) entity for the affected MCG.
*   **Release Connection:** Release the source connection (in the context of DAPS) or proceed to re-establishment.

**2. Recovery and Re-establishment**
The primary recovery mechanism is **RRC Re-establishment**.
*   **Procedure:** The UE initiates the RRC re-establishment procedure to re-establish the RRC connection with the network. This involves selecting a suitable cell and performing random access.
*   **Reporting:** After successful re-establishment (or upon entering RRC_IDLE/INACTIVE if re-establishment fails), the UE may report the RLF event to the network.
    *   The UE stores information in the **VarRLF-Report** variable, including the failed cell ID, the time elapsed since the failure, and the reconnection cell ID [E3].
    *   This information is included in the **RRCSetupComplete** message sent to the network after the RRC connection is re-established [E3].
    *   The report helps the network optimize mobility parameters and identify coverage issues [E3].

**3. Context Management**
*   **RRC Context:** The RRC layer is responsible for the recovery from radio link failure, which includes managing the transfer of RRC context information between network nodes if mobility occurs [E1].
*   **Security:** If the UE moves to a new cell or RAT during recovery, associated AS security handling (key/algorithm change) may be required [E1].

### Summary of Key Timers and Parameters
*   **N310:** Number of consecutive "out-of-sync" indications required to start T310.
*   **T310:** Timer started upon N310 out-of-sync indications; expiry triggers RLF.
*   **N311:** Number of consecutive "in-sync" indications required to stop T310 and recover from physical layer issues.
*   **T312:** Timer

evidence.text: ... Request from SMF, the SMF determines the 5QI and ARP based on the downlink packet (if the SMF performs buffering) or the Downlink Data Report received from UPF (if the UPF performs buffering). The SMF includes the 5QI and ARP corresponding to the QoS Flow of the received downlink PDU in the request sent to the AMF. If the UE is in CM IDLE, the AMF uses e.g. the 5QI and ARP to derive different paging strategies as described in clause 4.2.3.3 of TS 23.502 [3]. NOTE: The 5QI is used by AMF to determine suitable paging strategies. #### 5.4.3.2 Paging Policy Differentiation Paging policy differentiation is an optional feature that allows the AMF, based on operator configuration, to apply different paging strategies for different traffic or service types provided within the same PDU Session. In this Release of the specification this feature applies only to PDU Session of IP type. When the 5GS supports the Paging Policy Differentiation (PPD) feature, the DSCP value (TOS in IPv4 / TC in IPv6) is set by the application to indicate to the 5GS which Paging Policy should be applied for a certain IP packet. For example, as defined in TS 23.228 [15], the P-CSCF may support Paging Policy Differentiation by marking packet(s) to be sent towards the UE that relate to a specific IMS services (e.g. conversational voice as defined in IMS multimedia telephony service). NOTE 1: This PPD feature may be used to determine the Paging Cause Indication for Voice Service, as described in clause 5.38.3. It shall be possible for the operator to configure the SMF in such a way that the Paging Policy Differentiation feature only applies to certain HPLMNs, DNNs and 5QIs. In the case of HR roaming, this configuration is done in the SMF in the VPLMN. NOTE 2: Support of Paging Policy Differentiation in the case of HR roaming requires inter operator agreements including on the DSCP value associated with this feature. In the case of Network Triggered Service Request and UPF buffering downlink packets, the UPF shall include the DSCP in TOS (IPv4) / TC (IPv6) value from the IP header of the downlink packet and an indication of the corresponding QoS Flow in the Downlink Data Report sent to the SMF. When PPD applies, the SMF determines the Paging Policy Indicator (PPI) based on the DSCP received from the UPF. In the case of Network Triggered Service Request and SMF buffering downlink packets, when PPD applies, the SMF determines the PPI based on the DSCP in TOS (IPv4) / TC (IPv6) value ...

evidence.text: ... h RG connecting to 5GC, additional feature for IPv6 Prefix Delegation via DHCPv6 is defined in TS 23.316 [84]. #### 5.8.2.3 Management of CN Tunnel Info ##### 5.8.2.3.1 General CN Tunnel Info is the Core Network address of a N3/N9 tunnel corresponding to the PDU Session. It comprises the TEID and the IP address which is used by the UPF on the N3/N9 tunnel for the PDU Session. The CN Tunnel Info allocation and release is performed by the UPF. The SMF shall indicate to the UPF when the UPF is required to allocate/release CN Tunnel Info. ##### 5.8.2.3.2 Void ##### 5.8.2.3.3 Management of CN Tunnel Info in the UPF The UPF shall manage the CN Tunnel Info space. When a new CN Tunnel Info is needed, the SMF shall request over N4 the UPF to allocate CN Tunnel Info for the applicable N3/N9 reference point. In response, the UPF provides CN Tunnel Info to the SMF. In the case of PDU Session Release or a UPF is removed from the user plane path of an existing PDU Session, the SMF shall request UPF to release CN Tunnel Info for the PDU Session. If the corresponding N4 Session is released the UPF releases the associated CN Tunnel Info. #### 5.8.2.4 Traffic Detection ##### 5.8.2.4.1 General This clause describes the detection process at the UPF that identifies the packets belonging to a session, or a service data flow. The SMF is responsible for instructing the UP function about how to detect user data traffic belonging to a Packet Detection Rule (PDR). The other parameters provided within a PDR describe how the UP function shall treat a packet that matches the detection information. ##### 5.8.2.4.2 Traffic Detection Information The SMF controls the traffic detection at the UP function by providing detection information for every PDR. For IPv4 or IPv6 or IPv4v6 PDU Session type, detection information is a combination of: - CN tunnel info. - Network instance. - QFI. - IP Packet Filter Set as defined in clause 5.7.6.2. - Application Identifier: The Application Identifier is an index to a set of application detection rules configured in UPF. - FQDN Filter for DNS Query message. For Ethernet PDU Session type, detection information is a combination of: - CN tunnel info. - Network instance. - QFI. - Ethernet Packet Filter Set as defined in clause 5.7.6.3. In this Release of the specification for Unstructured PDU Session Type, the UPF does not perform-QoS Flow level traffic detection for QoS enforcement. Q4.answer:
In a 5G network, the handling of 5QI (5G QoS Identifier) and QoS Flows is a coordinated process between the control plane (specifically the SMF) and the user plane (UPF), governed by policy decisions from the PCF. The SMF acts as the central controller for session management and QoS enforcement, while the UPF executes the traffic detection and QoS treatment based on instructions from the SMF.

**Role of the SMF in 5QI and QoS Flow Management**

The Session Management Function (SMF) is responsible for determining the QoS parameters, including the 5QI, for each QoS Flow. This determination is driven by Policy and Charging Control (PCC) rules received from the Policy Control Function (PCF).

*   **QoS Flow Establishment and Binding:** The SMF binds PCC rules to QoS Flows. If a new QoS Flow is required, the SMF establishes it based on the binding parameters in the PCC rule. If a QoS Flow with identical QoS parameters already exists, the SMF may bind the new PCC rule to the existing flow rather than creating a new one, unless local policies or specific conditions (such as ensuring GBR achievement for delay-critical services) require a new flow [E4].
*   **Default QoS Rule Handling:** The SMF identifies the QoS Flow associated with the default QoS rule by matching the 5QI and Allocation and Retention Priority (ARP) values against the "Authorized default 5QI/ARP" provided in the PDU Session related information. If the authorized default 5QI cannot be used directly (e.g., if a GBR 5QI is required or priority levels need adjustment), the PCF can include a "Bind to QoS Flow associated with the default QoS rule" indication, forcing the SMF to bind the rule to the default flow regardless of other binding parameters [E4].
*   **Downlink QoS Determination:** When downlink data arrives, the SMF determines the 5QI and ARP for the corresponding QoS Flow. This determination is based on the downlink packet itself (if the SMF buffers the data) or a Downlink Data Report received from the UPF (if the UPF buffers the data) [E3]. The SMF then includes these 5QI and ARP values in requests sent to the Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF), which uses them to derive paging strategies [E3].

**Role of the UPF in Traffic Detection and QoS Enforcement**

The User Plane Function (UPF) executes the QoS policies by detecting user data traffic and applying the appropriate treatment. The SMF controls this process by providing specific detection and enforcement parameters to the UPF over the N4 interface.

*   **Traffic Detection:** The SMF instructs the UPF on how to detect user data traffic belonging to a Packet Detection Rule (PDR). For IP-based PDU Sessions, the detection information provided by the SMF includes a combination of:
    *   CN Tunnel Info (TEID and IP address).
    *   Network instance.
    *   QFI (QoS Flow Identifier).
    *   IP Packet Filter Set.
    *   Application Identifier (an index to internal application detection rules).
    *   FQDN Filter for DNS queries [E1].
*   **QoS Flow Identification:** The QFI is a key component of the traffic detection information. It allows the UPF to identify which QoS Flow a packet belongs to. For Ethernet PDU Sessions, the detection information similarly includes the QFI along with Ethernet Packet Filter Sets [E1].
*   **Downlink Data Reporting:** If the UPF buffers downlink packets (e.g., during a Network Triggered Service Request), it sends a Downlink Data Report to the SMF. This report includes the DSCP value from the IP header and an indication of the corresponding QoS Flow, enabling the SMF to determine the appropriate QoS parameters and paging policy [E3].
*   **Tunnel Management:** The UPF manages the Core Network Tunnel Info space. The SMF requests the UPF to allocate or release CN Tunnel Info (TEID and IP address) for N3/N9 reference points as needed for PDU Session establishment, modification, or release [E1].

**Interaction and Policy Context**

The "Authorised QoS" for a service data flow, which includes the 5QI and data rate, is defined as the maximum QoS authorized for that flow. When multiple service data flows are aggregated into a single QoS Flow, the "Authorised QoS" for the QoS Flow is the combination of the authorized QoS information of the individual flows [E2], [E5]. The SMF uses this authorized QoS information,

UE and serving network shall support EAP-AKA' and 5G AKA authentication methods. NOTE 2b: It is the home operator's decision which authentication method is selected. The USIM shall reside on a UICC. The UICC may be removable or non-removable. NOTE 3: For non-3GPP access networks USIM applies in case of terminal with 3GPP access capabilities. If the terminal supports 3GPP access capabilities, the credentials used with EAP-AKA' and 5G AKA for non-3GPP access networks shall reside on the UICC. NOTE 4: EAP-AKA' and 5G AKA are the only authentication methods that are supported in UE and serving network, hence only they are described in sub-clause 6.1.3 of the present document. For a private network using the 5G system as specified in [7] an example of how additional authentication methods can be used with the EAP framework is given in the informative Annex B. NOTE 5: For non-public network (NPN) security the Annex I of the present document provides details. Upon successful completion of the 5G AKA primary authentication, the AMF shall initiate NAS security mode command procedure (see clause 6.7.2) with the UE. NOTE 6: The reason to mandatory run the NAS SMC procedure after primary authentication is because the UE does not store the new derived $K_{AUSF}$ until receiving the NAS SMC message. The new partial native NAS security context is taken into use. It is specified in clause 6.9.4.4 whether AS key re-keying is performed. ### 6.1.1.2 EAP framework The EAP framework is specified in RFC 3748 [27]. It defines the following roles: peer, pass-through authenticator and back-end authentication server. The back-end authentication server acts as the EAP server, which terminates the EAP authentication method with the peer. In the 5G system, the EAP framework is supported in the following way: - The UE takes the role of the peer. - The SEAF takes the role of pass-through authenticator. - The AUSF takes the role of the backend authentication server. ### 6.1.1.3 Granularity of anchor key binding to serving network The primary authentication and key agreement procedures shall bind the $K_{SEAF}$ to the serving network. The binding to the serving network prevents one serving network from claiming to be a different serving network, and thus provides implicit serving network authentication to the UE. Q5.answer:
Based on the provided 3GPP technical evidence, the 5G authentication procedure is a mutual authentication process that establishes a secure key hierarchy between the User Equipment (UE) and the network. The procedure involves the interaction of the Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF), the Authentication Server Function (AUSF), and the Unified Data Management (UDM) [E5].

### 1. Roles of Network Functions

**Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF)**
*   **Security Anchor and Key Derivation:** The AMF (specifically its Security Edge Protection Proxy/SEAF component) acts as the pass-through authenticator in the EAP framework [E1]. It is responsible for deriving the serving network key ($K_{SEAF}$) and the AMF key ($K_{AMF}$) [E2].
*   **NAS Security Mode Command (SMC):** Upon successful primary authentication, the AMF initiates the NAS Security Mode Command procedure with the UE [E1]. This step is mandatory because the UE does not store the new derived $K_{AUSF}$ until it receives the NAS SMC message, at which point the new partial native NAS security context is taken into use [E1].
*   **Serving Network Binding:** The primary authentication procedure binds the $K_{SEAF}$ to the serving network, providing implicit serving network authentication to the UE [E1].

**Authentication Server Function (AUSF)**
*   **Backend Authentication Server:** In the EAP framework, the AUSF acts as the backend authentication server, terminating the EAP authentication method with the peer (UE) [E1].
*   **Key Management and Verification:** The AUSF requests authentication vectors (AVs) from the UDM, stores the expected response ($XRES^*$), and calculates the hash ($HXRES^*$) [E2]. It verifies the UE's response ($RES^*$) and provides the result and $K_{SEAF}$ to the SEAF/AMF [E2].
*   **Authentication Confirmation:** The AUSF informs the UDM of the authentication result (success or failure) and the time of the procedure using the `Nudm_UEAuthentication_ResultConfirmation` service operation [E3][E4].
*   **Stale Parameter Cleanup:** If a UE is authenticated by a new AUSF instance, the UDM may request the old AUSF to clear stale security parameters (such as $K_{AUSF}$ and counters) [E3].

**Unified Data Management (UDM)**
*   **Credential Storage and AV Generation:** The UDM (often in conjunction with the Authentication Repository and Processing Function, ARPF) generates the authentication vectors (AVs) used in the 5G AKA procedure [E2].
*   **Authentication Status Tracking:** The UDM stores the authentication status of the UE after receiving confirmation from the AUSF [E3][E4].
*   **Authorization of Subsequent Procedures:** The UDM uses the stored authentication status to authorize subsequent procedures, such as registration requests from the AMF [E3][E4].

### 2. 5G AKA Authentication Procedure

The 5G AKA procedure enhances EPS AKA by providing the home network with proof of successful authentication from the visited network [E2]. The sequence is as follows:

1.  **AV Generation:** The UDM/ARPF generates an Authentication Vector (AV) [E2].
2.  **AV Request:** The AUSF requests the AV from the UDM via the `Nudm_UEAuthentication_Get` service operation [E2].
3.  **AUSF Processing:** The AUSF stores the expected response ($XRES^*$) and calculates the hash $HXRES^*$ [E2].
4.  **Authentication Request:** The AUSF sends the 5G SE AV to the SEAF (AMF), which forwards an Authentication Request to the UE [E2].
5.  **UE Response:** The UE calculates the Authentication Response ($RES^*$) and sends it back to the SEAF [E2].
6.  **SEAF Verification:** The SEAF calculates $HRES^*$ and compares it to $HXRES^*$ [E2].
7.  **AUSF Verification:** The SEAF sends $RES^*$ to the AUSF via `Nausf_UEAuthentication_Authenticate` Request. The AUSF verifies $RES^*$ [E2].
8.  **Key Delivery:** The AUSF sends the result and $K_{SEAF}$ to the SEAF [E2].
9.  **NAS SMC:** The AMF initiates the NAS Security Mode Command to establish the security context [E1].
10. **Confirmation to UDM:** The AUSF sends `Nudm_UEAuthentication_Result

evidence.text: ### 1 Introduction QUIC is a multiplexed and secure transport protocol that runs on top of UDP. QUIC builds on past transport experience and implements mechanisms that make it useful as a modern general-purpose transport protocol. Using UDP as the substrate, QUIC seeks to be compatible with legacy clients and middleboxes. QUIC authenticates all of its headers, preventing middleboxes and other third parties from changing them, and encrypts most of its headers, limiting protocol evolution largely to QUIC endpoints only. This document describes the core QUIC protocol, including the conceptual design, wire format, and mechanisms of the QUIC protocol Internet-Draft QUIC October 2016 for connection establishment, stream multiplexing, stream and connection-level flow control, and data reliability. Accompanying documents describe QUIC's loss detection and congestion control [draft-iyengar-quic-loss-detection], and the use of TLS 1.3 for key negotiation [draft-thomson-quic-tls]. ### 2 Conventions and Definitions Definitions of terms that are used in this document: o Client: The endpoint initiating a QUIC connection. o Server: The endpoint accepting incoming QUIC connections. o Endpoint: The client or server end of a connection. o Stream: A logical, bi-directional channel of ordered bytes within a QUIC connection. o Connection: A conversation between two QUIC endpoints with a single encryption context that multiplexes streams within it. o Connection ID: The identifier for a QUIC connection. o QUIC packet: A well-formed UDP payload that can be parsed by a QUIC receiver. QUIC packet size in this document refers to the UDP payload size. ### 3 A QUIC Overview This section briefly describes QUIC's key mechanisms and benefits. Key strengths of QUIC include: o Low-latency Version Negotiation o Low-latency connection establishment o Multiplexing without head-of-line blocking o Authenticated and encrypted header and payload o Rich signaling for congestion control and loss recovery o Stream and connection flow control o Connection Migration and Resilience to NAT rebinding Internet-Draft QUIC October 2016 ### 3.1 Low-Latency Version Negotiation QUIC combines version negotiation with the rest of connection establishment to avoid unnecessary roundtrip delays. A QUIC client proposes a version to use for the connection, and encodes the rest of the handshake ...

... ndshake over TCP. For QUIC, this requires successful establishment of the QUIC connection with its integrated cryptographic handshake. *Connection Keep-Alive* Implementations SHOULD provide mechanisms to detect idle or failed connections and to prevent premature closure by network intermediaries. For TCP/TLS, implementations SHOULD utilize TCP keep-alive where appropriate. For QUIC, implementations SHOULD use QUIC-native liveness mechanisms, such as transport-level keep-alive signaling or PING frames, as provided by the implementation. Application-layer keep-alive messages MAY also be defined by future extensions for use across transport bindings. *Connection Re-establishment* If an active connection is unexpectedly terminated and continued interaction is required, IAIP entities SHOULD attempt to re-establish the connection. Re- establishment attempts MUST incorporate exponential back-off mechanisms to prevent congestion amplification or resource exhaustion. Under TCP/TLS, re-establishment is typically required after transport disruption. Under QUIC, re-establishment is required only if the QUIC connection itself has been lost; network path changes that are handled through QUIC connection migration do not constitute connection re-establishment. Implementations SHOULD preserve only the minimum state necessary to safely resume operation after reconnection. The AAC plays a critical role in managing session continuity and security-related state across connection disruptions. *Multiplexing* Multiple independent IAIP message exchanges MAY share a single persistent secure transport connection. Under TCP/TLS, such multiplexing occurs within the same protected byte stream and relies on unique MSG_ID and CORRELATION_ID fields for message correlation. Under QUIC, independent IAIP messages MAY be carried over different QUIC streams to reduce head-of-line blocking. In all cases, protocol-level correlation MUST rely on IAIP identifiers rather than on transport-level connection or stream identifiers alone. *Connection Migration and Path Changes* Transport bindings MAY differ in their ability to tolerate endpoint mobility or network path changes. TCP/TLS connections typically require re- establishment after a path-disrupting failure or endpoint address Internet-Draft IAIP May 2026 change. QUIC implementations MAY support connection migration in accordance with QUIC transport behavior, allowing continuity ...

### 4 Conventions and Definitions All integer values used in QUIC, including length, version, and type, are in little-endian byte order, and not in network byte order. QUIC does not enforce alignment of types in dynamically sized frames. A few terms that are used throughout this document are defined below. o "Client": The endpoint initiating a QUIC connection. o "Server": The endpoint accepting incoming QUIC connections. o "Endpoint": The client or server end of a connection. o "Stream": A bi-directional flow of bytes across a logical channel within a QUIC connection. Internet-Draft QUIC January 2016 o "Connection": A conversation between two QUIC endpoints with a single encryption context that multiplexes streams within it. o "Connection ID": The identifier for a QUIC connection. o "QUIC Packet": A well-formed UDP payload that can be parsed by a QUIC receiver. QUIC packet size in this document refers to the UDP payload size. ### 5 A QUIC Overview We now briefly describe QUIC's key mechanisms and benefits. QUIC is functionally equivalent to TCP+TLS+HTTP/2, but implemented on top of UDP. Key advantages of QUIC over TCP+TLS+HTTP/2 include: o Connection establishment latency o Flexible congestion control o Multiplexing without head-of-line blocking o Authenticated and encrypted header and payload o Stream and connection flow control o Forward error correction o Connection migration ### 5.1 Connection Establishment Latency QUIC combines the crypto and transport handshakes, reducing the number of roundtrips required for setting up a secure connection. QUIC connections are commonly 0-RTT, meaning that on most QUIC connections, data can be sent immediately without waiting for a reply from the server, as compared to the 1-3 roundtrips required for TCP+TLS before application data can be sent. QUIC provides a dedicated stream (Stream ID 1) to be used for performing the handshake, but the details of this handshake protocol are out of this document's scope. For a complete description of the current handshake protocol, please see the QUIC Crypto Handshake [3]document. QUIC current handshake will be replaced by TLS 1.3 in the future. Key advantages of QUIC over TCP+TLS+HTTP/2 include: o Connection establishment latency o Flexible congestion control o Multiplexing without head-of-line blocking Internet-Draft QUIC July 2016 o Authenticated and encrypted header and payload o Stream and connection flow control o Connection migration ### 3.1 Connection Establishment Latency QUIC combines the crypto and transport handshakes, reducing the number of roundtrips required for setting up a secure connection. QUIC connections are commonly 0-RTT, meaning that on most QUIC connections, data can be sent immediately without waiting for a reply from the server, as compared to the 1-3 roundtrips required for TCP+TLS before application data can be sent. QUIC provides a dedicated stream (Stream ID 1) to be used for performing the handshake, but the details of this handshake protocol are out of this document's scope. For a complete description of the current handshake protocol, please see the QUIC Crypto Handshake [2]document. QUIC current handshake will be replaced by TLS 1.3 in the future. ### 3.2 Flexible Congestion Control QUIC has pluggable congestion control and richer signaling than TCP, which enables QUIC to provide richer information to congestion control algorithms than TCP. Currently, the default congestion control is a reimplementation of TCP Cubic; we are currently experimenting with alternative approaches. One example of richer information is that each packet, both original and retransmitted, carries a new packet sequence number. This allows a QUIC sender to distinguish ACKs for retransmissions from ACKs for original transmissions, thus avoiding TCP's retransmission ambiguity problem. QUIC ACKs also explicitly carry the delay between the receipt of a packet and its acknowledgment being sent, and together with the monotonically-increasing packet numbers, this allows for precise roundtrip-time (RTT) calculation. Finally, QUIC's ACK frames support up to 256 ack blocks, so QUIC is more resilient to reordering than TCP (with SACK), as well as able to keep more bytes on the wire when there is reordering or loss. Based on the provided technical evidence, QUIC is a multiplexed and secure transport protocol that operates over UDP, designed to be functionally equivalent to TCP+TLS+HTTP/2 while addressing specific limitations of legacy protocols [E1][E3][E4]. The protocol authenticates and encrypts most headers to prevent middlebox interference and limits protocol evolution to the endpoints [E1][E5].

The key mechanisms of QUIC, specifically regarding connection establishment, stream multiplexing, and connection migration, are detailed below.

### 1. Connection Establishment
QUIC significantly reduces connection establishment latency by integrating the cryptographic and transport handshakes [E3][E4].

*   **Reduced Roundtrips (0-RTT):** Unlike TCP+TLS, which typically requires 1–3 roundtrips before application data can be sent, QUIC connections are commonly 0-RTT (zero roundtrip time) [E3][E4]. This allows data to be sent immediately without waiting for a server reply in many cases [E3][E4].
*   **Integrated Handshake:** The protocol combines version negotiation with the rest of the connection establishment to avoid unnecessary roundtrip delays [E1]. A dedicated stream (Stream ID 1) is used to perform the handshake [E3][E4].
*   **Security Integration:** QUIC uses TLS 1.3 for key negotiation [E1]. The handshake is integrated into the transport layer, meaning the establishment of a secure connection requires the successful establishment of the QUIC connection itself [E2].
*   **Header Protection:** From the Handshake encryption level, QUIC control information, including packet numbers and frame formats, is authenticated and encrypted [E5]. This protects against transport-layer attacks such as packet injection or reset attacks that are possible with TCP [E5].

### 2. Stream Multiplexing
QUIC provides multiplexing without head-of-line (HoL) blocking, a key advantage over TCP-based multiplexing (such as HTTP/2 over TCP) [E1][E3][E4].

*   **Logical Channels:** A QUIC connection is defined as a conversation between two endpoints with a single encryption context that multiplexes multiple streams [E1][E3]. A stream is a logical, bi-directional channel of ordered bytes within a connection [E1][E3].
*   **Independence:** Independent messages or data flows can be carried over different QUIC streams [E2]. This isolation ensures that the loss or delay of data in one stream does not block the delivery of data in other streams, thereby reducing head-of-line blocking [E2][E5].
*   **Reliability and Datagrams:** QUIC supports both reliable streams and unreliable datagrams [E5]. This dual capability allows the protocol to support various application needs, including real-time media and port forwarding for both UDP and TCP-based protocols [E5].
*   **Flow Control:** QUIC implements both stream-level and connection-level flow control to manage data throughput and prevent congestion [E1][E3][E4].

### 3. Connection Migration
QUIC supports connection migration, which provides resilience to network path changes and endpoint mobility, a feature not natively supported by TCP [E1][E3][E4][E5].

*   **Path Change Tolerance:** QUIC implementations can support connection migration in accordance with QUIC transport behavior, allowing continuity of the connection when the network path changes [E2].
*   **Mobility Support:** A mobile host roaming between networks can maintain established connections alive by migrating them to a newly acquired IP address [E5]. This avoids disrupting active sessions (such as remote terminals or media streams) upon network changes [E5].
*   **Distinction from Re-establishment:** Network path changes handled through QUIC connection migration do not constitute connection re-establishment [E2]. Re-establishment is only required if the QUIC connection itself is lost [E2].
*   **NAT Resilience:** QUIC is designed to be resilient to NAT rebinding, allowing connections to persist even when the underlying network address changes [E1].

### Additional Mechanisms
*   **Congestion Control and Loss Recovery:** QUIC features pluggable congestion control and richer signaling than TCP [E3][E4]. Each packet carries a new sequence number, allowing senders to distinguish acknowledgments for retransmissions from original transmissions, thus avoiding TCP's retransmission ambiguity [E4]. QUIC ACKs explicitly carry delay information for precise RTT calculation and support up to 256 acknowledgment blocks, making it more resilient to reordering than TCP [E4].
*   **Keep-Alive:** Implementations should use QUIC-native liveness mechanisms, such as transport-level keep-alive signaling or PING frames, to detect idle connections and prevent premature closure by network intermediaries [E2

evidence.text: ... l loops, remain largely absent from existing literature. Several studies explore ML approaches for content caching but in non-industrial contexts. For instance, [5] and [13] examine RL-based popularity prediction and adaptation primarily for video streaming, not addressing mission-critical reliability or safety constraints essential to IIoT. Similarly, [11], [12], and [14] discuss learning-enabled caching for vehicular and immersive VR scenarios but do not examine collaborative intelligence architectures or inference-aware policies specific to industrial automation, predictive maintenance, or digital twin synchronization. Recent surveys have advanced understanding of complementary areas: collaborative caching strategies for general edge computing [21], deep learning for fog/edge caching optimization [22], distributed ML execution on edge devices [23], ML-driven cache management innovations [24], mobile edge intelligence for LLMs [25], and proactive IoT caching architectures [26]. However, these works focus on consumer-oriented or general edge computing contexts without addressing the unique Industry 5.0 requirements of sub-millisecond safety response, regulatory compliance (IEC 61508, ISO 10218), and multi-stage workflow dependencies that distinguish industrial edge intelligence from conventional edge caching. Overall, although ML-driven edge caching has attracted significant research attention, including recent comprehensive surveys in IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials on distributed machine learning [17], federated edge computing, and intelligent caching architectures, existing works continue to focus predominantly on consumer, mobile, and multimedia applications [11], [17], or provide broad taxonomies and architectural perspectives [13], [16] without systematically examining the collaborative, distributed, and inference-enabled caching strategies necessary for industrial edge intelligence in Industry 5.0 contexts. While distributed ML techniques are well-covered in recent literature, their application to industrial caching problems with domain-specific constraints such as sub-millisecond safety requirements, multi-stage workflow dependencies, and regulatory compliance remains largely unexplored. As a result, three fundamental Industry 5.0 requirements remain underexplored: ultra-low inference latency for edge analytics, information freshness for control applications, and collaborative multi-agent coordination for distributed operations. For instance, [5] and [13] examine RL-based popularity prediction and adaptation primarily for video streaming, not addressing mission-critical reliability or safety constraints essential to IIoT. Similarly, [11], [12], and [14] discuss learning-enabled caching for vehicular and immersive VR scenarios but do not examine collaborative intelligence architectures or inference-aware policies specific to industrial automation, predictive maintenance, or digital twin synchronization. Recent surveys have advanced understanding of complementary areas: collaborative caching strategies for general edge computing [21], deep learning for fog/edge caching optimization [22], distributed ML execution on edge devices [23], ML-driven cache management innovations [24], mobile edge intelligence for LLMs [25], and proactive IoT caching architectures [26]. However, these works focus on consumer-oriented or general edge computing contexts without addressing the unique Industry 5.0 requirements of sub-millisecond safety response, regulatory compliance (IEC 61508, ISO 10218), and multi-stage workflow dependencies that distinguish industrial edge intelligence from conventional edge caching. Overall, although ML-driven edge caching has attracted significant research attention, including recent comprehensive surveys in IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials on distributed machine learning [17], federated edge computing, and intelligent caching architectures, existing works continue to focus predominantly on consumer, mobile, and multimedia applications [11], [17], or provide broad taxonomies and architectural perspectives [13], [16] without systematically examining the collaborative, distributed, and inference-enabled caching strategies necessary for industrial edge intelligence in Industry 5.0 contexts. While distributed ML techniques are well-covered in recent literature, their application to industrial caching problems with domain-specific constraints such as sub-millisecond safety requirements, multi-stage workflow dependencies, and regulatory compliance remains largely unexplored. As a result, three fundamental Industry 5.0 requirements remain underexplored: ultra-low inference latency for edge analytics, information freshness for control applications, and collaborative multi-agent coordination for distributed operations. Q7.answer:
Based on the provided technical evidence, the use of AI/ML-based traffic prediction and analytics in mobile network management offers significant performance benefits but introduces distinct technical and operational challenges.

### Main Benefits

1.  **Proactive Resource Allocation and Congestion Mitigation**
    AI/ML systems enable predictive scheduling by analyzing historical and real-time data to forecast future demand. This allows the network to proactively allocate resources before congestion occurs, rather than reacting to it after the fact [E1]. This proactive approach is critical for maintaining Quality of Service (QoS) and enhancing user experience [E1].

2.  **Enhanced Network Performance Metrics**
    The integration of ML in Radio Resource Management (RRM) and scheduling leads to measurable improvements in key performance indicators. Specifically, these systems improve spectral efficiency (SE), increase overall network capacity, and reduce latency [E1]. By continuously monitoring metrics such as throughput, Signal-to-Interference-plus-Noise Ratio (SINR), and packet loss, ML models can dynamically adjust resource allocation to optimize these parameters in real time [E1].

3.  **Interference-Aware Optimization**
    ML techniques can identify complex interference patterns that may be difficult to detect with static rules. By learning these patterns, the system can adjust radio access decisions to minimize interference, thereby improving signal quality and resource utilization [E1].

4.  **Self-Adaptive and Prescriptive Network Behavior**
    Leveraging data analytics and ML allows networks to become "self-aware" and "self-adaptive." This enables the network to not only react to current conditions but also provide prescriptive actions for coverage and capacity optimization, including load balancing, mobility management, and beam-forming [E2].

5.  **Improved Network Slicing and Edge Computing**
    In the context of 6G and edge computing, AI/ML facilitates efficient network slicing by predicting node states and optimizing resource slicing for specific service requirements [E4]. It also supports the deployment of privacy-preserving models at the edge, improving scalability and deployment flexibility for distributed learning tasks [E4].

### Technical Challenges

1.  **Data Availability and Labeling Constraints**
    The effectiveness of ML models depends heavily on the availability of data. The choice between supervised, reinforcement, or federated learning strategies is constrained by the availability of labeled data and the dynamics of the environment [E1]. In many mobile network scenarios, obtaining high-quality, labeled datasets for training is a significant hurdle.

2.  **Real-Time Processing and Latency Requirements**
    For applications requiring ultra-low latency (such as industrial IoT or mission-critical services), the inference time of ML models at the edge becomes a critical challenge. Existing literature notes that while distributed ML is well-covered, its application to problems with sub-millisecond safety response times and strict information freshness requirements remains underexplored and technically demanding [E3].

3.  **Complexity of Deployment and Scalability**
    Deploying ML models in a distributed manner (e.g., at the network edge) introduces challenges related to scalability, containerization, and resource constraints on edge devices. While techniques like Federated Learning (FL) and containerization (Docker/Kubeadm) are being explored to address privacy and deployment flexibility, the integration of these systems into existing network architectures remains complex [E4].

4.  **Generalization and Domain-Specific Constraints**
    Many current ML studies focus on consumer-oriented or general edge computing contexts (e.g., video streaming, VR). Applying these models to specific domains with unique constraints—such as regulatory compliance (IEC 61508, ISO 10218) or multi-stage workflow dependencies in industrial automation—remains a gap in the literature [E3]. This suggests that general-purpose traffic prediction models may not directly translate to specialized network management scenarios without significant adaptation.

5.  **Integration with Emerging Technologies**
    There is a noted lack of elaboration on how Deep Learning (DL) concepts can be tailored for emerging networking technologies such as Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) [E2]. Bridging the gap between advanced ML algorithms and the specific architectural requirements of these next-generation network layers is an ongoing research challenge.

In summary, while AI/ML-based traffic prediction significantly enhances the efficiency, capacity, and responsiveness of mobile networks, its practical implementation is limited by data constraints, real-time inference latency, and the difficulty of generalizing models across diverse and highly constrained network environments.

### Appendix B ATLS and HTTP CONNECT It is worthwhile comparing and contrasting ATLS with HTTP CONNECT tunneling. First, let us introduce some terminology: o HTTP Proxy: A HTTP Proxy operates at the application layer, handles HTTP CONNECT messages from clients, and opens tunnels to remote origin servers on behalf of clients. If a client establishes a tunneled TLS connection to the origin server, the HTTP Proxy does not attempt to intercept or inspect the HTTP messages exchanged between the client and the server o middlebox: A middlebox operates at the transport layer, terminates TLS connections from clients, and originates new TLS connections to services. A middlebox inspects all messages sent between clients and services. Middleboxes are generally completely transparent to applications, provided that the necessary PKI root Certificate Authority is installed in the client's trust store. HTTP Proxies and middleboxes are logically separate entities and one or both of these may be deployed in a network. HTTP CONNECT is used by clients to instruct a HTTP Forward Proxy deployed in the local domain to open up a tunnel to a remote origin server that is typically deployed in a different domain. Assuming that TLS transport is used between both client and proxy, and proxy and origin server, the network architecture is as illustrated in Figure 16. Once the proxy opens the transport tunnel to the service, the client establishes an end-to-end TLS session with the service, and the proxy is blindly transporting TLS records (the C->S TLS session records) between the client and the service. From the client perspective, it is tunneling a TLS session to the service inside the TLS session it has established to the proxy (the C->P TLS session). No middlebox is attempting to intercept or inspect the HTTP messages between the client and the service. evidence.text: ### Appendix B ATLS and HTTP CONNECT It is worthwhile comparing and contrasting ATLS with HTTP CONNECT tunneling. First, let us introduce some terminology: o HTTP Proxy: A HTTP Proxy operates at the application layer, handles HTTP CONNECT messages from clients, and opens tunnels to remote origin servers on behalf of clients. If a client establishes a tunneled TLS connection to the origin server, the HTTP Proxy does not attempt to intercept or inspect the HTTP messages exchanged between the client and the server o middlebox: A middlebox operates at the transport layer, terminates TLS connections from clients, and originates new TLS connections to services. A middlebox inspects all messages sent between clients and services. Middleboxes are generally completely transparent to applications, provided that the necessary PKI root Certificate Authority is installed in the client's trust store. HTTP Proxies and middleboxes are logically separate entities and one or both of these may be deployed in a network. HTTP CONNECT is used by clients to instruct a HTTP Forward Proxy deployed in the local domain to open up a tunnel to a remote origin server that is typically deployed in a different domain. Assuming that TLS transport is used between both client and proxy, and proxy and origin server, the network architecture is as illustrated in Figure 16. Once the proxy opens the transport tunnel to the service, the client establishes an end-to-end TLS session with the service, and the proxy is blindly transporting TLS records (the C->S TLS session records) between the client and the service. From the client perspective, it is tunneling a TLS session to the service inside the TLS session it has established to the proxy (the C->P TLS session). No middlebox is attempting to intercept or inspect the HTTP messages between the client and the service. NOTE: When using TCP as the transport protocol, an HTTP/2 connection is mapped to a TCP connection. If a Network Function does not register any port number to the NRF then it shall be prepared to receive connections on default port numbers, i.e. TCP port 80 for "http" URIs and TCP port 443 for "https" URIs as specified in IETF RFC 9113 [7]. ## 5.4 Serialization Protocol The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format as described in IETF RFC 8259 [10] shall be used as serialization protocol. The content of JSON attributes of string type shall be encoded as UTF-8. For transmitting large parts of opaque binary data along with JSON format, multipart messages shall be supported using: - A multipart/related media type; - 3gpp vendor specific content subtype; and - Cross-referencing from the JSON content using the Content-ID field. Use of multipart messages is documented in specific specifications. ## 5.5 Interface Definition Language OpenAPI Specification [9] shall be used as Interface Definition Language (IDL) of SBI. --- # 6 General Functionalities in Service Based Architecture ## 6.1 Routing Mechanisms ### 6.1.1 General This clause specifies the generic routing mechanisms in the 5GC. Specific requirements to support Indirect communication are further defined in clause 6.10. For HTTP message routing between Network Functions, the message routing mechanism as specified in clause 7 of IETF RFC 9110 [11] is almost followed with some differences due to the adoption of HTTP/2 and to some 5G system specificities. NOTE: The term "inbound" are defined in clause 3.7 of IETF RFC 9110 [11]. It describes a directional requirement in relation to the request route: "inbound" means toward the origin server. ### 6.1.2 Identifying a target resource The target resource is identified by a target URI (e.g. a Resource URI, a Custom operation URI or a Callback URI as defined in clause 4.4 of TS 29.501 [5]). ### 6.1.3 Connecting inbound If the request is not satisfied by a local cache, then the client shall connect to an authority server for the target resource or to a proxy. NOTE: When using TCP as the transport protocol, an HTTP/2 connection is mapped to a TCP connection. If a Network Function does not register any port number to the NRF then it shall be prepared to receive connections on default port numbers, i.e. TCP port 80 for "http" URIs and TCP port 443 for "https" URIs as specified in IETF RFC 9113 [7]. ## 5.4 Serialization Protocol The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format as described in IETF RFC 8259 [10] shall be used as serialization protocol. The content of JSON attributes of string type shall be encoded as UTF-8. For transmitting large parts of opaque binary data along with JSON format, multipart messages shall be supported using: - A multipart/related media type; - 3gpp vendor specific content subtype; and - Cross-referencing from the JSON content using the Content-ID field. Use of multipart messages is documented in specific specifications. ## 5.5 Interface Definition Language OpenAPI Specification [9] shall be used as Interface Definition Language (IDL) of SBI. --- # 6 General Functionalities in Service Based Architecture ## 6.1 Routing Mechanisms ### 6.1.1 General This clause specifies the generic routing mechanisms in the 5GC. Specific requirements to support Indirect communication are further defined in clause 6.10. NOTE: The term "inbound" are defined in clause 3.7 of IETF RFC 9110 [11]. In the 5G Service-Based Architecture (SBA), communication between Network Functions (NFs) is facilitated using HTTP and TLS as the underlying transport and security mechanisms. The 3GPP specifications define the functional roles, service interfaces, and message semantics for NFs such as the Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF) and Session Management Function (SMF), while the IETF standards define the generic transport protocols (HTTP) and security protocols (TLS) used to carry these messages.

**1. 3GPP Defined Roles and Service Interfaces**

The 5G System (5GS) Control Plane utilizes Service-Based Interfaces (SBIs) to enable direct or indirect communication between NFs [E3]. These interfaces are defined by 3GPP specifications that outline the specific services exposed by each NF.

*   **AMF (Access and Mobility Management Function):** The AMF is responsible for access and mobility management. It exposes services to other NFs via specific SBIs. For example, the AMF communicates with the SMF via the `Namf` interface and with the Authentication Server Function (AUSF) via the `Nausf` interface [E3]. The AMF also interacts with the Policy Control Function (PCF) via `Npcf` and the Network Slice Selection Function (NSSF) via `Nnssf` [E3].
*   **SMF (Session Management Function):** The SMF is responsible for session management. It exposes services to the AMF via the `Nsmf` interface and to the User Plane Function (UPF) via the `N4` interface (which is a reference point, not strictly an SBI in the same sense as control plane SBIs, but part of the management/control interaction) [E3]. The SMF also interacts with the Unified Data Management (UDM) via `Nudm` and the Application Function (AF) via `Naf` [E3].
*   **Service Definitions:** The specific services and message formats for these interfaces are defined in 3GPP TS 29.501 (Principles and Guidelines for Services Definition) and TS 29.502 (Session Management Services) [E1]. These documents specify the RESTful API structure, resource models, and message payloads that NFs must implement.

**2. IETF Defined Transport and Security Mechanisms**

The 3GPP SBA mandates the use of IETF-standardized protocols for the actual transmission of these service messages.

*   **HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol):** The transport layer for SBA communication is HTTP. The IETF defines HTTP semantics and versions in RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1), RFC 9113 (HTTP/2), and RFC 9114 (HTTP/3) [E5]. 3GPP specifications reference these IETF standards to ensure interoperability. The use of HTTP allows for RESTful API interactions, where NFs expose resources that can be accessed via standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) [E4][E5].
*   **TLS (Transport Layer Security):** Security for SBA communication is provided by TLS. The IETF defines TLS in RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) [E1][E5]. TLS provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication for the HTTP messages exchanged between NFs. The use of TLS ensures that the service-based interfaces are protected against eavesdropping and tampering.

**3. Distinction Between 3GPP and IETF Roles**

*   **3GPP (Functional and Semantic Layer):** 3GPP defines *what* is communicated and *who* communicates with *whom*. It specifies the NF roles (AMF, SMF, etc.), the service interfaces (Namf, Nsmf, etc.), the resource models, and the business logic associated with 5G services [E1][E3]. 3GPP TS 29.501 and TS 29.502 provide the normative definitions for the services exposed by NFs [E1].
*   **IETF (Transport and Security Layer):** IETF defines *how* the messages are transported and secured. It provides the generic protocols (HTTP, TLS) that are agnostic to the specific 5G service content. The IETF standards ensure that the transport mechanisms are robust, interoperable, and secure, but they do not define the 5G-specific service semantics [E4][E5].

**4. Integration in 5G SBA**

In practice, when an AMF needs to communicate with an SMF, it constructs an HTTP request containing a JSON payload defined by 3GPP TS 29.502 (or related service specifications) [E1]. This

Thus, multi-dimensional data types should be combined to identify the best RAN configuration for the optimization of the QoE per user. evidence.text: ... risk of untrusted communication due to weak mutual authentication, where a malicious E2 Node or Near-RT RIC may communicate over the E2 interface, leading to unauthorized access and potential exploitation. Malicious actors could also monitor messaging across the E2 interface, enabling MITM attacks to read sensitive information exchanged between nodes, and attackers could modify or inject messages, causing the Near-RT RIC or E2 Nodes to receive malicious or altered messages, potentially disrupting operations or compromising data integrity. These vulnerabilities highlight the importance of implementing robust authentication and encryption mechanisms to protect the E2 interface's communication integrity, confidentiality, and availability. This aligns with the overarching Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) approach adopted by the O-RAN Alliance, which assumes that adversaries may already be present within the network. ## 3) A1 INTERFACE The A1 interface connects the Non-RT RIC, which is located in the SMO layer, with the Near-RT RIC in the RAN and designed to support a multi-vendor environment and be extensible for future enhancements. Its primary objective is to enable policy-based guidance and provide enrichment information to optimize RAN performance in alignment with specified Service Level Agreement (SLA)s. A1 interface has two main functions [69]: 1) Policy Management (A1-P): This function allows the Non-RT RIC to create, modify, and delete A1 policies that guide the Near-RT RIC in achieving RAN intent. These policies can be tailored for individual or groups of UEs. 2) Enrichment Information (A1-EI): This function is responsible for the discovery, request, and delivery of enrichment information, enhancing the Near-RT RIC's operational capabilities by providing additional context and data. Security measures and considerations for the A1 interface are described in [70]. The A1 interface aligns with ZTA principles, meaning that Near-RT RIC does not automatically trust incoming policies or data but instead validates them against defined schemas and value ranges to ensure integrity and authenticity. The interface employs TLS to encrypt data, ensuring confidentiality and integrity against eavesdropping and tampering. For an A1 policy to be effective, it must have a valid policy type recognized by Near-RT RIC and be mapped to an xApp, which ensures that only authorized policies can influence xApps. evidence.text: ... bles the creation of tailored virtual networks for various applications, ranging from low-latency autonomous vehicle communication to high-speed urban broadband [58]. Fig. 5 illustrates the functional architecture of the RIC, which is divided across the Non-RT and Near-RT domains. It highlights how policy flows from high-level, long-term decisions in the SMO/Non-RT RIC, through the A1 interface, into rapid-response xApps in the Near-RT RIC over the E2 interface. This structured separation enables scalable, policy-driven automation while supporting time-sensitive operations near the DU/RU. By visualizing the coordination layers and control interfaces, the latency-sensitive decisions are split between centralized analytics and distributed real-time enforcement, a foundational principle for closed-loop RAN automation. The Near-RT RIC, operating with response times ranging from 10 ms to 1 s, is responsible for near-real-time network adjustments, including traffic steering, interference management, and radio resource optimization. It ensures that users experience smooth connectivity, whether they're streaming, gaming, or on a call. Meanwhile, the Non-RT RIC, which works on a longer timescale, analyzes network behavior, applies AI-driven optimizations, and makes predictive adjustments to improve efficiency over time [58]. Beyond performance enhancements, the RIC also strengthens network security and energy efficiency. It detects and mitigates cyber threats in real-time, reducing the risk of disruptions. At the same time, it optimizes power consumption by adjusting network resources in response to demand, making future networks more intelligent and sustainable. Both RIC components rely on open interfaces, allowing them to interact seamlessly with different vendors' hardware and software, making networks more adaptable, scalable, and future-proof [58]. As wireless technology advances, the RIC will remain at the core of next-generation networks, driving the industry toward AI-powered, software-defined, and highly flexible infrastructures. It ensures that mobile connectivity continues to meet the increasing demands of users, businesses, and emerging technologies, shaping a smarter, more efficient wireless future. ## #### 1) SERVICE MANAGEMENT FOR NON-RT RIC SMO is a platform enabling automation for the resources of the O-RAN. The architectural distinction between O-RAN rApps and xApps is fundamentally defined by their association with different Radio Intelligent Controllers (RICs), their operational timescales, and their specific roles within the hierarchical control loop.

**Architectural Differences: rApps vs. xApps**

1.  **Hosting Environment and Timescale:**
    *   **xApps (Near-RT RIC):** xApps are hosted within the **Near-RT RIC**, which operates on a timescale of **10 ms to 1 s** [E1], [E5]. These applications are designed for time-sensitive, near-real-time control tasks such as load balancing, handover optimization, and interference mitigation [E1].
    *   **rApps (Non-RT RIC):** rApps are hosted within the **Non-RT RIC**, which operates on a timescale **greater than 1 s** [E1], [E4]. The Non-RT RIC is functionally internal to the Service Management and Orchestration (SMO) framework [E4]. rApps focus on long-term optimization, AI/ML model training, and high-level policy management [E1], [E4].

2.  **Functional Scope and Granularity:**
    *   **xApps:** Focus on rapid-response network adjustments, including traffic steering, radio resource optimization, and ensuring smooth connectivity for user experiences (e.g., streaming, gaming) [E5]. They execute control actions based on real-time telemetry from the RAN.
    *   **rApps:** Provide RAN optimization and operations at a higher level of abstraction, including policy guidance, enrichment information, configuration management, and data analytics [E4]. rApps can influence a large number of users and perform management and orchestration tasks that are not feasible at the millisecond scale [E4]. While rApps can support similar control functionalities as xApps, they do so at a larger timescale [E4].

3.  **Interface Connectivity:**
    *   **xApps:** Interact with the RAN (O-CU/O-DU) via the **E2 interface** [E1].
    *   **rApps:** Interact with the SMO and other RAN elements via **O1** and **O2** interfaces, and communicate with the Near-RT RIC via the **A1 interface** [E1], [E4].

**Role of A1 and E2 Interfaces**

The A1 and E2 interfaces facilitate a hierarchical control structure where long-term policies guide short-term actions.

**1. A1 Interface: Policy Guidance and Enrichment**
The A1 interface connects the Non-RT RIC (in the SMO) to the Near-RT RIC [E3], [E4]. It operates on a timescale of seconds or above [E1] and serves two primary functions:
*   **Policy Management (A1-P):** The Non-RT RIC uses A1 to create, modify, and delete policies that guide the Near-RT RIC in achieving specific RAN intents or Service Level Agreements (SLAs) [E3]. These policies can be tailored for individual or groups of User Equipment (UEs) [E3]. For a policy to be effective, it must be mapped to a specific xApp, ensuring that only authorized policies influence the near-real-time control logic [E3].
*   **Enrichment Information (A1-EI):** This function allows the Non-RT RIC to provide additional context and data to the Near-RT RIC, enhancing its operational capabilities [E3]. This includes AI/ML model updates and data that O1/O2 interfaces might not capture, such as specific E2 data needed for rApp logic [E1], [E2].

**2. E2 Interface: Near-Real-Time Control**
The E2 interface connects the Near-RT RIC to the E2 Nodes (O-CU and O-DU) [E1]. It operates on a timescale of **10 ms to 1 s** [E1].
*   **Control and Telemetry:** The E2 interface enables the Near-RT RIC to perform near-real-time control actions, such as load balancing and interference mitigation, and to collect telemetry data from the RAN [E1].
*   **xApp Execution:** xApps use the E2 interface to execute their control logic based on the policies received via A1 and the real-time telemetry from the RAN [E1], [E5].

**Synthesis: Hierarchical Optimization**
The O-RAN architecture enables a closed-loop control system where the Non-RT RIC (via rApps) analyzes long-term network behavior and generates policies/enrichment information via A1. The Near-RT RIC (via xApps) consumes this guidance and applies it to real-time RAN operations via E2. This separation allows for scalable, policy-driven automation, where

There are also projects like [node-healthcheck-operator](https://github.com/medik8s/node-healthcheck-operator) that can be used for some scenarios. We expect developments in this area from hardware vendors and cloud providers, and we expect to see mostly DIY solutions in the near future. The cheapness is mostly coming from reuse of pre-allocated resources as much as possible. From reusing the Pods by restarting containers in-place, to node local restart of containers instead of rescheduling whenever possible, to snapshotting support, and re-scheduling prioritizing the same node to save on image pulls. Consider this scenario: A big training job needs 512 Pods to run. And one of the pods failed. It means that all Pods need to be interrupted and synced up to restart the failed step. The most efficient way to achieve this generally is to reuse as many Pods as possible by restarting them in-place, while replacing the failed pod to clear up the error from it. Like demonstrated in this picture: {{< figure src="inplace-pod-restarts.svg" alt="The picture shows 512 pod, most ot them are green and have a recycle sign next to them indicating that they can be reused, and one Pod drawn in red, and a new green replacement Pod next to it indicating that it needs to be replaced." >}} It is possible to implement this scenario, but all solutions implementing it are fragile due to lack of certain extension points in Kubernetes. Adding these extension points to implement this scenario is on the Kubernetes roadmap. ### Roadmap for failure modes: device degradation There is very little done in this area - there is no clear detection signal, very limited troubleshooting tooling, and no built-in semantics to express the "degraded" device on Kubernetes. There has been discussion of adding data on device performance or degradation in the ResourceSlice used by DRA to represent devices, but it is not yet clearly defined. There are also projects like [node-healthcheck-operator](https://github.com/medik8s/node-healthcheck-operator) that can be used for some scenarios. We expect developments in this area from hardware vendors and cloud providers, and we expect to see mostly DIY solutions in the near future.
